transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-06
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Recording: zoom link (redacted)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (Willowgate HoP), Tom Garvey (Cloud Architect), Leila Ortiz (Security), Ben Cho (Product)

Summary:
Quick discovery to validate network onramp and security controls for a Private/VPC deployment of Redwood inference. Focus on VPC peering versus PrivateLink, transit gateway design, IP ranges, egress constraints, SOC2/KMS needs, and timeline for a pilot.

Topics (auto):
- Onramp options (VPC peering, PrivateLink, Transit Gateway)
- IP addressing and NAT/egress requirements
- Region gating and data residency
- Authentication, KMS, audit logs, SSO
- Benchmarks and rollout plan

Action items: see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, i'll kick us off. we are excited to talk about how Redwood can fit into Willowgate's private onramp. quick intros?
[00:12] Priya Raman: hi i'm priya, head of platform at Willowgate. we're evaluating options to run inference inside our VPCs for financial workloads, lots of regional restrictions.
[00:20] Tom Garvey: tom here cloud architect, i'll own the network side.
[00:24] Leila Ortiz: leila, security. we'll need to see SOC2, pen test and KMS integration details.
[00:29] Ben Cho: ben, product, mostly here for success criteria and timeline.
[00:33] Maya Chen: great thanks. diego from our infra team?
[00:36] Diego Alvarez: hey all, hi i'm diego, i'll take the deep network and deployment Qs. quick note: i'll share a design doc after the call.
[00:44] Priya Raman: perfect. high level constraints for us: must stay in EU and us-east region for different data types, can't cross certain country borders, and we need private endpoints—no public internet egress for inference traffic.
[00:58] Maya Chen: understood, region gating is common. we support Private (VPC) deployments per region and you can pin model versions to a regionized runtime. you mentioned no public egress—do you have an on-prem proxy for third party egress or everything is fully air-gapped?
[01:17] Priya Raman: not air gapped, but egress is tightly controlled. outbound to vendor endpoints needs to go through our egress proxy; we prefer PrivateLink or VPC peering with static IPs on Redwood side if possible.
[01:31] Diego Alvarez: quick clarification — when you say static IPs you mean you'll want an allowlist of IPs on your side for Redwood endpoints, correct?
[01:36] Tom Garvey: yes, and we need to avoid NAT that obscures client IPs for audit logging reasons.
[01:44] Leila Ortiz: also TTL retention for logs, we need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[01:49] Maya Chen: got it. our Private product can be deployed with PrivateLink endpoints, or we can set up VPC peering. tradeoffs: PrivateLink (AWS) -> simpler for restricted egress, integrates with our private endpoint; VPC peering -> lower latency but you have to handle routing and there's cross-account peering management; transit gateway -> good at scale when you have many VPCs.
[02:11] Ben Cho: is there any reason to prefer dedicated vs private for our use case?
[02:15] Diego Alvarez: Dedicated is reserved capacity in our shared control plane; it's still hosted in Redwood network and might require fewer network changes, but for strict data residency and network isolation Private (VPC) is the route. also Private gives you full control over network egress paths.
[02:31] Priya Raman: we are leaning Private because compliance folks won't sign off on hosted APIs that leave our network perimeter.
[02:38] Maya Chen: makes sense. on the networking details, can you share your VPC CIDRs, whether you use transit gateway, and if you require cross-region peering?
[02:48] Priya Raman: we'll share that post-call. currently primary workload sits in eu-west-1 and us-east-1, we use AWS Transit Gateway and have a central egress VPC.
[02:57] Tom Garvey: and we use route 53 private zones for internal discovery. any DNS requirements on Redwood side?
[03:04] Diego Alvarez: we can support private DNS with PrivateLink; we can also publish the endpoint ip ranges if you prefer peering. note: sometimes our automation picks ephemeral ip ranges for autoscaling, we can provision static elastic IPs for the NAT gateway in front of the service if needed.
[03:20] Leila Ortiz: the important part is we need preserved source IPs for audit events and MFA-based SSO for engineers. how does Redwood handle audit logs and identity?
[03:30] Maya Chen: we support SSO via SAML/Okta with RBAC, plus we can stream audit logs to your syslog or S3 (encrypted). our Private control plane can be configured to forward kinesis-like audit events; i'll include diagram and sample retention config.
[03:44] Ben Cho: and how about key management? we need customer-managed keys for model inputs at rest, or at least for any persisted artifacts.
[03:52] Diego Alvarez: we support CMK via AWS KMS for Private deployments. for runtime memory we don't persist inputs unless you opt-in for logging or debugging; snapshots/artifacts can be encrypted with your KMS key.
[04:06] Priya Raman: ok good. what's the typical network setup? we were imagining a transit gateway peering to Redwood accounts, or set up PrivateLink endpoints in our VPC. what are pros/cons?
[04:18] Maya Chen: pros/cons: Transit Gateway: centralizes routing if you have many VPCs, good for enterprise scale; requires us to peer into your TGW attachment or you share a TGW—there's some cross-account setup. PrivateLink: simpler for per-VPC connections, fully private, and integrates with private DNS; limited if you need high bandwidth between multiple VPCs. VPC Peering: low latency and simple for few VPCs but scales poorly.
[04:39] Tom Garvey: bandwidth—our inference traffic could be significant, are there throughput caps on PrivateLink?
[04:45] Diego Alvarez: PrivateLink itself is bounded by ENI throughput; for high throughput we recommend Transit Gateway or peering and colocating inference close to your application. we can size and propose autoscaling pools. i'll add a throughput table to the doc.
[04:58] Priya Raman: and egress IPs—will you provide a stable block? we need to put that into our firewall rules for the egress proxy.
[05:06] Maya Chen: yes we can provide an allowlist of fixed IPs per region or set up an ENI-backed interface with fixed elastic IPs. there's an ops step but it's doable.
[05:15] Leila Ortiz: what about certificate management and TLS termination? we need TLS inside our private network and mutual TLS for service-to-service?
[05:23] Diego Alvarez: we support mTLS for service-to-service in Private deployments if you want—mutual TLS using certs you control or via our managed certs. for S3 artifact endpoints we use TLS + sigv4.
[05:36] Ben Cho: you mentioned KV cache and batching optimizations in your docs—does that impose any stateful connectivity requirements?
[05:44] Maya Chen: the KV cache is ephemeral per runtime instance; it doesn't require external state unless you opt to share the cache across regions. batching happens at the runtime layer, no special network ports beyond normal HTTPS. sometimes the transcript generator garbles product names as "K V cash" but that's just transcription.
[06:03] Priya Raman: timeline — we are hoping for a pilot in 6 weeks. what's a typical onboarding path for private?
[06:11] Maya Chen: typical path: 1) network intake and IP/CIDR exchange, 2) security review and SOC2 docs, 3) pilot deployment in a single region (we provide an infra-as-code module), 4) testing/benchmarks with your prompts, 5) rollout to additional regions. usually 4-8 weeks depending on approvals.
[06:30] Tom Garvey: for the infra-as-code module, do you support terraform or cloudformation?
[06:34] Diego Alvarez: we provide Terraform modules and CloudFormation templates for the Private onramp. we also have a kustomize helm chart for on-prem.
[06:43] Leila Ortiz: on the audit side, retention: we need 12 months by default, and the ability to forward to our SIEM—can you log token-level events?
[06:52] Maya Chen: we can log per-request metadata (token counts, latencies, model version) and send them to your S3 or Splunk. we redaction sensitive fields by default and only retain raw inputs if you opt in.
[07:06] Ben Cho: any known regulatory gotchas for finance customers in EU?
[07:11] Diego Alvarez: data residency and data-in-transit are the main ones. if you have PII we recommend model pinning to EU regions and ensuring KMS in that region. also watch out for cross-border backups.
[07:25] Priya Raman: are there special SLAs for Private deployments?
[07:29] Maya Chen: we offer SLA-backed Dedicated plans; Private deployments include an uptime and latency SLO in the contract; for strict SLAs we usually do a signed Enterprise agreement.
[07:40] Priya Raman: ok good. can you run a small benchmark against our prompt set? we have some low-latency 2-3 token bursts and some long form 8k prompts.
[07:50] Diego Alvarez: yes we can run a bench if you share sample prompts and expected QPS. for long-form 8k we might suggest a quantized variant and a slightly larger GPU to keep latency acceptable. i'll scope the bench after i see the prompt set.
[08:03] Tom Garvey: network security: do you require any inbound ports other than for the private endpoint? firewall team wants a list.
[08:09] Diego Alvarez: only standard HTTPS ports for the PrivateLink interface; if using peering there's no inbound public ports. i'll send an allowlist with ports and CIDR.
[08:18] Leila Ortiz: incident response: who do we call for P1? what's the escalation path?
[08:22] Maya Chen: for Enterprise we have 24/7 oncall and a PagerDuty integration; contact details will be in the contract, and our CSM will be the initial POC.
[08:32] Ben Cho: curious about model versioning—if we pin a model version in eu-west; can we have a fallback to a different quantized model in us-east if capacity is hit?
[08:42] Diego Alvarez: yes our routing supports model variants and fallback policies: you can configure route by region, latency or cost and automatic fallback to compatibile variant. we'll show configuration examples.
[08:54] Priya Raman: costs—do you have rough ballparks for per-token cost in a private deployment vs hosted?
[08:59] Maya Chen: private has higher fixed infra cost but lower variable egress and better predictable throughput; i'll have diego put together a rough TCO for pilot vs hosted.
[09:08] Tom Garvey: can we do a hybrid where training and sensitive data stay on-prem but inference runs in Redwood private in our VPC?
[09:15] Diego Alvarez: yes that's a common pattern—training/data residency vs inference serving. as long as the data exchange is over your private links with encryption and KMS controls, that works.
[09:25] Priya Raman: any pre-existing bank customers you can name as references?
[09:29] Maya Chen: we can provide references under an NDA—i'll arrange that.
[09:35] Leila Ortiz: final question, penetration test — do you allow customers to run tests against the private endpoints?
[09:41] Diego Alvarez: yes, with coordination. we have a scheduled window and requirements for scope; we'll share the pen test policy doc.
[09:50] Ben Cho: cool. i think that covers the main list. do you want to run through next steps?
[09:55] Maya Chen: sure. recap: 1) Priya to share CIDRs, transit gateway ids, and sample prompt set. 2) Maya to send security packet and SOC2 link. 3) Diego to produce latency/cost ballpark and throughput table and network allowlist. 4) schedule design workshop for 2026-04-13.
[10:16] Priya Raman: yes we'll get that to you by end of next week.
[10:20] Maya Chen: perfect, we'll follow up with deck and terraform examples + security links: https://redwood.example.com/security/willowgate-packet (placeholder), and a design doc: https://drive.example.com/redwood/willowgate-design (placeholder).
[10:35] Tom Garvey: thanks everyone.
[10:37] Leila Ortiz: thanks.
[10:38] Maya Chen: thanks all, talk soon.
[10:40] END OF RECORDING
